claim: Out “with verbs of motion is restricted to source”, so She went out of the room is “(source, not goal)”.
evidence_summary: Ch. 4, p. 284 [35iib], has I must put the cat out (of the house). Put takes an obligatory goal: Ch. 7, p. 605, cites “the goal complement of certain transitive verbs such as put or place”, with ∗I put it, and Ch. 8, p. 685, counts put among the “causative verbs of movement”. In [35iib] out is the only element that could fill that goal.
finding: Medium-low confidence. If out in [35iib] is put’s goal, the restriction needs an exception for causative verbs of movement. Reading out (of the house) as a source with an implicit goal is hard to square with put’s obligatory goal. Page 687 itself admits other source and direction prepositions as goals “under restricted conditions” (Place it well away from the fire).
inference: Is out restricted to source with verbs of motion?

evidence.passage: §4.3, p. 687. “A different kind of exception is out, which with verbs of motion is restricted to source”.
evidence.example: Ch. 4, p. 284 [35iib] I must put the cat out (of the house); Ch. 7, p. 605 [6i].
evidence.establishes: The book’s own example appears to have out filling put’s obligatory goal.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.
